points.title: Showing that one past event happened before another one

teach.can_do: I can show my listener which of two past events happened first, without having to spell the order out.
teach.why_it_matters: Stories and explanations both double back at some point. Without this form the reader has to guess the order and usually guesses wrong.
teach.meaning: Ordinary past tense lays events down in the order you say them. The past perfect breaks that arrangement. It reaches back behind a moment the telling has already fixed and puts an earlier event there. You need it when you have walked your listener to a point in the past and then have to explain something that was already true, already finished, or already going wrong before that point arrived. It is not about distance. It is about which of two past moments you are measuring from.

notes: had never changes for the subject: I had gone, she had gone, they had gone
'd in speech and in a letter: she'd left before the call came
'd is also the short form of would, so the shape of the next word decides which one you heard
form.question: Had you + past participle ... ?

marks.label: the moment the story has reached
now, which this form says nothing about

spec.caption: The past perfect is not further back on its own. It is further back than a point the telling has already fixed.

worked_example.sentence: When the relief driver reached the yard, the depot had sent the load out by road.
worked_example.why_this_form: The telling has stopped at the driver's arrival. The load went out behind that moment, so the sentence has to reach back past the point it is standing on.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Sent would line the two up in the order given: the driver turns up, and then the load goes out. That is a different afternoon.

notice_set.sentence: When we got to the platform, the Marlow train had left.
notice_set.question: Did we see the train go?

notice_set.sentence: When we got to the platform, the Marlow train left.
notice_set.question: Did we see the train go?
notice_set.why: Both events sit on the same line in the order given, so the train went while we watched.

notice_set.sentence: The council cancelled the scheme. It had cost eleven million pounds.
notice_set.question: Which came first?
notice_set.why: The second sentence steps back behind the first one in order to explain it.

notice_set.sentence: Rasheed was furious because nobody had told him about the change.
notice_set.question: Had anyone spoken to him before he found out?
notice_set.why: The conversation that never happened is placed behind the anger, which is what makes the anger make sense.

notice_set.sentence: The ferry had been out of service for three weeks when the storm hit.
notice_set.question: Was the ferry running on the day of the storm?
notice_set.why: The three weeks are measured backwards from the storm, so they were over by the time it arrived.

notice_set.sentence: Delia moved to Sandmouth in 2016. She had trained as a baker in Verdon.
notice_set.question: Where did she learn the trade?
notice_set.why: The training is set behind the move, so it belongs to the life she had before she arrived.

teach.rule_line: Ask: has my telling already reached a later moment that this event happened before?
teach.false_rule: That the past perfect means a long time ago. It says nothing about distance. It says only: earlier than the moment we are standing on.

errors.right: When the auditors arrived, the depot had destroyed the old rotas.

errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: had.

errors.wrong: First she had studied engineering at Verdon, and then she worked in Ashfield.
errors.right: First she studied engineering at Verdon, and then she worked in Ashfield.

errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: had.

errors.wrong: The depot shut in March. The last two drivers had left in January, and the site had stood empty ever since.
errors.right: The depot shut in March. The last two drivers had left in January, and the site has stood empty ever since.
errors.why_it_happens: Once the step back is switched on it tends to stay on for the rest of the paragraph. The writer stops asking, clause by clause, which moment each verb is measured from.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: had becomes has.

errors.wrong: He said he never worked a night shift before that week.
errors.right: He said he had never worked a night shift before that week.
errors.why_it_happens: The reporting verb has already put the sentence in the past, so a second past-marked verb feels like repetition. The experience being reported is older than the saying, and nothing shows it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: had.

points.title: Deciding when you actually need to show which past event came first

point_json.grammar_name: Past perfect vs past simple in a sequence

teach.can_do: I can tell when the step back into the past perfect is doing work, and when it is only weight.
teach.why_it_matters: Learners are taught to use this form and never taught to stop. Sprinkling it through a story is as visible as leaving it out.
teach.meaning: The past perfect is not a courtesy you pay to every earlier event. It exists to fix an order the sentence would otherwise get wrong. If a time word, or the plain order of the telling, already puts the events in sequence, the reader has everything they need and the extra auxiliary adds nothing but drag. Reach for it when you are genuinely going back out of sequence: a flashback, an explanation found after the effect, a reason that was in place before anybody noticed it.

form.pattern: had + past participle, but only where the order is not already visible
notes: before, after and then carry the order themselves, so the past simple is usually enough beside them
a plain list of events told in the order they happened needs no step back at all
once the step back is made, the following clauses in the same flashback can go back to the past simple
form.negative: hadn't + past participle — the same test applies; a negative is not a reason to use it
form.question: Had it happened by then? — asked when you want the state of things at an earlier moment

left.text: She finished the report and then went home.

right.text: She went home. She had finished the report at four.

spec.caption: Same two events, same real order. Only one version needs an auxiliary to say so.

worked_example.sentence: The surveyor refused to sign. Someone had changed the figures on the second page.
worked_example.why_this_form: The refusal comes first in the telling and second in time. Without the step back the reader files the changing as the next thing that happened.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Changed would read as a reply to the refusal, as though the figures were altered afterwards to get round it.

notice_set.sentence: The driver checked the load and then locked the van.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: Then does the whole job. Nothing needs marking, because the telling and the timing already agree.

notice_set.sentence: The van was empty when it reached Marlow. Somebody had unlocked it overnight.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: The telling has gone backwards, and the auxiliary is the only thing telling the reader so.

notice_set.sentence: After the funding stopped, the clinic reduced its opening hours.
notice_set.question: Can you tell which came first?
notice_set.why: After settles it on its own, which is why nothing else has to be marked.

notice_set.sentence: Rasheed apologised at the meeting. He had read the wrong version of the report.
notice_set.question: Did he read the wrong version before or after apologising?
notice_set.why: The second sentence is the explanation, and explanations sit behind the thing they explain.

notice_set.sentence: Rasheed apologised at the meeting. He read the wrong version of the report.
notice_set.question: Did he read the wrong version before or after apologising?
notice_set.why: With nothing marking a step back, the second sentence reads as the next thing he did.

discovery.prompt: Half of these would be worse with an extra auxiliary in them, and half would be wrong without one. What separates them?
pairs: The van was empty. Somebody had unlocked it overnight.
The driver checked the load and then locked the van.
She refused to sign. Someone had altered the figures.
She altered the figures and then refused to sign.
The clinic cut its hours. The grant had run out in April.

candidate_rules.text: The left-hand sentences go back out of the order they are told in; the right-hand ones do not.
The left-hand sentences are about problems and the right-hand ones are about routine actions.
Use had whenever a sentence contains two past events.

teach.rule_line: Ask: would the reader get the order wrong without it?
teach.false_rule: That the earlier of two past events always takes the past perfect. Most of the time the order is already visible and the auxiliary is dead weight.

contrast.question: Would the order be clear without the auxiliary?

fork.answer: Yes — a time word, or the order of the telling, already fixes it
No — the telling has doubled back and nothing else marks it

a.text: The engineer left the site and the alarm went off.
a.means: She was gone, and then the alarm sounded. Two events in the order given.

b.text: The engineer left the site and the alarm had gone off.
b.means: The alarm sounded first, and her leaving is being explained by it.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You reached back with had while the sentence was walking forwards. The reader now hunts for the later moment you are measuring from, fails to find one, and reads the sentence twice before giving up on it.

edge_case.text: In a long narrative you do not have to keep making the step. One past perfect opens the flashback and the past simple can carry the rest of it. Mark the door, not every room inside.

contrast.stronger_test: Cover the auxiliary and read the sentence again. If the order still comes out right, the auxiliary was decoration.

worked_pairs.b: The last delivery arrived at four and the shop closed at six.

errors.why_it_happens: The learner has learned that this form marks earlier events, and every event in a list is earlier than the next. Nothing in that rule says the list needs a later moment to lean on.

errors.wrong: First the council had cut the subsidy, and then the operator withdrew the route.

errors.why_it_happens: First and then have already sequenced the sentence. The learner marks the earlier verb anyway, because the rule they carry is about order rather than about what the reader can already see.

errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: had.

points.title: Using a whole statement as the subject or object of a sentence

teach.can_do: I can put a whole statement into a sentence as if it were a single noun.
teach.why_it_matters: It is how you state a position without opening with I think. Every stance sentence in an essay is built on it.
teach.meaning: Most sentences take a noun as their subject and another noun as their object. A that-clause lets a whole statement do either job. The claim that the scheme saved money can be the thing you are talking about; that the scheme saved money can be the thing somebody shows, argues or doubts. Nothing changes inside the statement — it keeps its own subject and its own verb — but the sentence around it now handles it as one lump, and can hang a verb on it.

form.pattern: that + subject + verb, filling a noun-sized slot
notes: as the object of a reporting verb, that can be dropped in speech: he says the road is closed
as the subject the clause is usually pushed to the end, and it holds the front: it is clear that costs have risen
the fact that turns the clause into a noun phrase, which is what lets it follow a preposition
form.negative: The negative goes inside the clause: it is clear that costs have not fallen.
form.question: Is it clear that ...? — the question is asked of the main verb, never of the clause.

left.role: a noun in the object slot
left.text: The report showed a sharp rise.

right.role: a whole statement in the same slot
right.text: The report showed that costs had risen sharply.

spec.caption: One slot, two things that can fill it. The clause is doing a noun's job.

worked_example.sentence: It is widely accepted that class size matters less to results than teacher quality does.
worked_example.why_this_form: The claim is the thing being discussed, so it needs a noun slot, and it carries too much to be squeezed into a noun phrase.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The effect of class size on results names the topic but drops the claim, and the sentence stops asserting anything at all.

notice_set.sentence: The audit showed that the figures had been copied from the previous year.
notice_set.question: What did the audit show?
notice_set.why: The whole statement is the thing the audit showed, which is why it sits where a noun would.

notice_set.sentence: That the trial was stopped early surprised nobody.
notice_set.question: What surprised nobody?
notice_set.why: The clause is the subject here. It is what the sentence is about.

notice_set.sentence: It is unlikely that the funding will be renewed.
notice_set.question: Is the funding expected to continue?
notice_set.why: It holds the subject slot for the clause, and the clause carries the whole prediction.

notice_set.sentence: The fact that two departments measure the same thing differently has never been raised.
notice_set.question: How many departments measure it?
notice_set.why: The clause has been packed into a noun phrase so that the sentence can hang a verb on it.

notice_set.sentence: She admitted the deadline was impossible.

points.title: Saying what one thing gets somebody else to do

teach.can_do: I can say that one thing causes, allows or persuades somebody else to act.
teach.why_it_matters: Most of an essay about policy is sentences about what a rule makes people do. Without this pattern you write two clauses where one carries more.
teach.meaning: A group of very common verbs takes two things after it: a person or thing, and then an action with to in front of it. Allow, encourage, force, enable, persuade, require, expect, remind, cause. The object names who acts; the infinitive names what they do. Between them they pack a cause and its effect into one clause, and the reader sees the link instead of having to build it. The object is part of the pattern, not an optional extra.

notes: the object is never dropped: allow people to work, not allow to work
the passive keeps the to: drivers are encouraged to use the park-and-ride
make and let break this pattern by dropping the to — they are handled in their own point
form.negative: The negative sits on the infinitive: the rules allow staff not to attend.
form.question: What does the scheme encourage people to do?

right.text: to leave the car at home

spec.caption: The verb names the pressure. The object names who feels it. The infinitive names the result.

worked_example.sentence: Charging for the centre encourages commuters to leave the car at the edge of town.
worked_example.why_this_form: The charge and the behaviour are one causal move, and the pattern keeps them in one clause where the reader can see the join.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The centre charges drivers, so they leave the car states two facts and hands the reader the job of connecting them.

notice_set.why: Required names the pressure; the developer is the one under it.

notice_set.sentence: Poor lighting caused two drivers to miss the turning.

notice_set.why: The subject supplies the cause. The object supplies the person who actually did the thing.

notice_set.sentence: Staff are expected to report faults the same day.
notice_set.question: Who reports faults?
notice_set.why: In the passive the object has moved to the front, but it is still the one who acts.

notice_set.sentence: The grant enabled the clinic to open on Saturdays.

notice_set.why: Enable says the action became possible, so it was not happening before.

teach.rule_line: Name the pressure, then who feels it, then what they do.
teach.false_rule: That you can say allow to do something. This group of verbs will not skip the person; the object is part of the pattern, not an option.

errors.wrong: The new rules allow to work from home two days a week.
errors.right: The new rules allow staff to work from home two days a week.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner is treating allow as a one-word permission verb, which is how the equivalent verb works in many first languages. English wants to know who is being allowed before it will take the action.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: staff.
errors.l1_note: Common where the equivalent verb takes only an action.

errors.wrong: The council encouraged residents recycle more of their waste.
errors.right: The council encouraged residents to recycle more of their waste.
errors.why_it_happens: The object arrives correctly and then the action follows bare, on the model of make and let. Those two are the exception; everything else in this group needs the to.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: to.

errors.wrong: Higher fares caused many passengers switching to the bus.
errors.right: Higher fares caused many passengers to switch to the bus.
errors.why_it_happens: Result in takes an -ing form, and cause sits beside it in the learner's mental list of result verbs. The two look interchangeable and take different shapes.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: switching becomes to switch.

errors.wrong: A policy which requires every household to separate food waste.
errors.right: A policy which requires every household to separate food waste has been in place since 2019.
errors.why_it_happens: The pattern is long enough to feel like a finished sentence, and the writer runs out of attention before the main verb ever arrives.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one main verb after the pattern.

enable residents to move

points.title: Saying why you did something, without using because

point_json.grammar_name: Infinitive of purpose vs for + noun

teach.can_do: I can say what something is for, and pick the marker the sentence actually wants.
teach.why_it_matters: For plus an -ing form to express a person's purpose is one of the commonest errors in the module, and it survives all the way up to band 7.
teach.meaning: English has two ways of saying what something is for, and they are not swappable. To plus a bare verb answers why did you do it: it names an action you were aiming at. For plus a noun answers what is it for: it names the function of a thing or the group it is meant for. The difference is not formality and it is not length. It is whether what follows is an action somebody performed or a job something does.

form.pattern: to + base verb (an aim) / for + noun (a function or a beneficiary)
notes: never for to: for cannot introduce an infinitive at all
for plus -ing names what a thing is generally used for, not why a person acted once
in order to and so as to are the same structure, longer and more formal
form.negative: so as not to + verb, or in order not to + verb; a bare not to is ambiguous
form.question: What did you go there to do?

left.text: She went to Verdon to study engineering.

right.text: The back room is for storage.

spec.caption: One names the aim of a person. The other names the function of a thing.

worked_example.sentence: Many students take an extra year to improve their English before applying.
worked_example.why_this_form: Improving is what the students were aiming at, so the sentence needs an action, and to plus a verb is how English attaches one.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: For improving would turn the year into a piece of equipment with a stated function, and the student disappears from their own sentence.

notice_set.sentence: She moved to Ashfield to look after her mother.
notice_set.question: Why did she move?
notice_set.why: To plus a verb names the aim behind the move.

notice_set.sentence: This card is for the staff car park.
notice_set.question: Is the card doing something, or being used for something?
notice_set.why: For plus a noun names the job the object does.

notice_set.sentence: He took the early train to avoid the roadworks.
notice_set.question: What was the point of the early train?
notice_set.why: The infinitive gives the reason behind the choice.

notice_set.sentence: The hall is used for exams in June.
notice_set.question: Who sits the exams, according to this sentence?
options: People, though the sentence does not name them
notice_set.why: For plus a noun names a function and leaves the people out of it.

notice_set.sentence: She rang the office to check the closing time.
notice_set.question: What did she want?
options: To find out when it closes
To tell them when it closes
notice_set.why: The infinitive gives her aim, not a fact about the office.

discovery.prompt: Each pair describes the same situation from two sides. Work out what the marker in front is doing.
pairs: He joined the club to meet people.
The club is for people new to the town.
She saved for a year to buy a van.
The fund is for equipment, not wages.
They rebuilt the shed to store the tools.

candidate_rules.text: To plus a verb names an action somebody was aiming at; for plus a noun names the job a thing does.
To is used with people and for is used with buildings.
Use for whenever the word after it ends in -ing.

teach.rule_line: If what follows is an action you were aiming at, use to plus a verb.
teach.false_rule: That for and to are two ways of saying the same thing and you pick whichever sounds better. For will not carry an infinitive at all.

contrast.question: Is what comes next an action somebody aimed at?

fork.answer: Yes — somebody did it in order to achieve something
No — it is the function of a thing, or the group it is meant for

a.text: I came to the centre to learn Spanish.
a.means: Learning Spanish is my aim, and I am the one doing it.

b.text: I came to the centre for Spanish lessons.
b.means: Lessons are the service I came for. What I do there is not stated.

minimal_pair.only_difference: to learn Spanish / for Spanish lessons

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote for learning Spanish. That reads as a label on a room or a line in a budget, not as something you set out to do. Your own aim has quietly turned into a category of use.

edge_case.text: For plus -ing is perfectly correct when you are naming what a tool or a space is used for: this knife is for boning fish. It is only wrong when it has been put in the place of a person's aim.

contrast.stronger_test: Put in order in front of it. If in order to works, the sentence wanted an infinitive, because in order for is not English here.

worked_pairs.a: She stayed late to finish the accounts.
worked_pairs.b: She stayed late for the overtime.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first names what she was doing. The second names what she was after.

worked_pairs.a: The council widened the path to reduce accidents.
worked_pairs.b: The council widened the path for cyclists.
worked_pairs.gloss: An aim and a beneficiary are different things, and each takes its own marker.

worked_pairs.a: I use this app to track my spending.
worked_pairs.b: I use this app for budgeting.
worked_pairs.gloss: Both are correct. The first says what I do with it; the second names the category of use.

errors.wrong: I came to this college for to improve my writing.
errors.right: I came to this college to improve my writing.
errors.why_it_happens: For and to both feel necessary because the learner's first language marks purpose with a single word that covers both. English uses one marker at a time.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: for.
errors.l1_note: Very common where one word covers both markers.

errors.wrong: She took the extra module for improving her chances of a place.
errors.right: She took the extra module to improve her chances of a place.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows that a preposition takes an -ing form and applies that rule correctly. The problem is a step earlier: a person's aim is not a function, so the preposition should not be there at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one phrase: for improving becomes to improve.

errors.wrong: This room is used to storage.
errors.right: This room is used for storage.
errors.why_it_happens: Used to is stored whole as a phrase about past habits and arrives instead of the preposition the sentence actually needs.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: to becomes for.

errors.wrong: The gate was locked for prevent people crossing the yard.
errors.right: The gate was locked to prevent people crossing the yard.
errors.why_it_happens: For is being treated as a joining word that can take a verb. It is a preposition, and prepositions take nouns or -ing forms, never a bare verb.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: for becomes to.

payload.stem: The app was built ___ energy use in older houses.

options.why_this_means: That tracking energy use is what the developers set out to make it do.
That tracking energy use is the job it does, stated as a function rather than as anyone's aim.

feedback.why_key: Both are correct, because a built thing has an aim behind it and a function in front of it. They are two true sentences.

items.decision_cue: for reducing traffic in the centre

payload.sentence: Several cities have raised parking charges for reducing traffic in the centre.
reasons: an aim behind an action needs to plus a verb
the main verb should be in the past
the preposition should be with
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.feed_forward: Swap for plus -ing to to plus a verb when a person or a body acted.

payload.sentence: Many learners join a conversation group for to practise speaking outside class.

expected: to practise
to practice
in order to practise

feedback.why_key: Two purpose markers are stacked, and English keeps the one that can carry a verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete for and keep to.

payload.prompt_text: Somebody asks why you are studying English. Answer in one sentence that names an aim rather than a subject.

feedback.why_key: An aim turns a flat fact about your timetable into a reason the listener can follow.
feedback.feed_forward: Attach to plus a verb to the thing you did.

points.title: Choosing between -ing and to when the choice changes what you mean

point_json.grammar_name: Verbs whose meaning changes with the pattern

teach.can_do: I can hear the difference between stopping to do something and stopping doing it, and say the one I mean.
teach.why_it_matters: These are not two ways of saying the same thing. The wrong one produces a perfectly clear sentence reporting the opposite of what happened.
teach.meaning: With most verbs, choosing -ing or to is a matter of which pattern the verb happens to take, and nothing turns on it. With a small set it is a meaning switch. The -ing form points backwards at something already real: an act done, a habit running, an activity in progress. The to-form points forwards at something planned, attempted, or still to come. Same verb, two directions in time, two different events for the listener to picture.

form.pattern: verb + -ing (already real) / verb + to (ahead or intended)
notes: stop doing ends the activity; stop to do breaks off from something else in order to start it
remember doing is a memory of the act; remember to do is a duty that did not slip
forget doing means no memory of it; forget to do means it never happened
try doing tests a method; try to do attempts something difficult
regret doing wishes it undone; regret to say frames bad news you are about to give
go on doing continues the same thing; go on to do moves to the next thing
mean doing names a consequence; mean to do names an intention
form.negative: Negatives go on the second verb: he remembered not to sign, she regrets not asking.
form.question: Did you stop to read it, or stop reading it? Those are two different afternoons.

ends: planned or attempted, ahead of you

marks.label: stop reading, remember posting, regret saying, mean losing
stop to read, remember to post, regret to say, mean to lose

worked_example.sentence: She stopped answering emails at six and started again after dinner.
worked_example.why_this_form: Answering is the activity that ended, and the -ing form points back at something that was already running when the stopping happened.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Stopped to answer would say she broke off from something else in order to start answering, which is the opposite arrangement of her evening.

notice_set.sentence: He stopped reading the report.
notice_set.question: Was he reading before this moment?
notice_set.why: The -ing form points back at an activity that was already running.

notice_set.sentence: I remember locking the gate.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker saying the gate got locked?
notice_set.why: The memory is of the act itself, so the act happened.

notice_set.sentence: She forgot to send the invoice.
notice_set.question: Was the invoice sent?
notice_set.why: Forget plus to names a duty that never got done at all.

notice_set.sentence: Try adding a second coat.
notice_set.question: Is this about a method, or about something difficult?
notice_set.why: Try plus -ing offers an experiment: see whether this works.

notice_set.sentence: We regret to inform you that the post has been filled.
notice_set.question: When is the bad news being delivered?
notice_set.why: Regret plus to is the polite frame around news the writer is delivering right now.

notice_set.sentence: Building the bypass would mean losing eight hectares of woodland.
notice_set.question: Is losing the woodland a plan or a consequence?
notice_set.why: Mean plus -ing names what something would involve, not what anybody intends.

discovery.prompt: Each pair uses the same verb and describes two different afternoons. Work out what the two forms are doing.
pairs: He stopped to read the report.
She remembered to post the form.
They went on arguing about the budget.
They went on to argue about the budget.

candidate_rules.text: The -ing form points back at something already real; the to-form points forward to something intended or next.
The -ing form is used for long actions and the to-form for short ones.
Use -ing after a past tense verb and to after a present tense one.

teach.rule_line: Ask whether the second verb is already real or still ahead.
teach.false_rule: That these verbs take both patterns freely, so either is safe. With this set the pattern is the meaning, and the wrong one is a clear sentence about a different event.

contrast.question: Is the second verb already real, or still ahead?

fork.answer: Already real — it happened, or it was running at the time
Still ahead — intended, attempted, or the next move

a.means: The reading ended. He was doing it, and now he is not.

b.text: He stopped to read the report.
b.means: Something else ended so that the reading could start.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote stopped to read. That says he broke off from whatever he was doing in order to begin reading. If the reading is what ended, you have reported the afternoon backwards, and the sentence is clear enough that nobody will query it.

edge_case.text: Outside this small set the choice carries no meaning at all: enjoy takes -ing and decide takes to, and there is nothing to work out. Learn the set; leave the rest to the vocabulary card.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask whether the second verb had already happened at the moment of the first one. If it had, the -ing form is the one.

worked_pairs.b: She remembered to post the form.
worked_pairs.gloss: In the first the form is in the post and she has the memory. In the second the memory came first and the form went afterwards.

worked_pairs.a: Try turning it off and on again.
worked_pairs.b: Try to turn it off without unplugging anything.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first offers a method that might work. The second names something awkward and asks for the attempt.

worked_pairs.a: They went on arguing about the budget for another hour.
worked_pairs.b: They went on to argue that the budget was never realistic.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first is the same argument continuing. The second is the next thing they did after finishing something else.

errors.wrong: I stopped to smoke three years ago and I feel much better.
errors.right: I stopped smoking three years ago and I feel much better.
errors.why_it_happens: Stop is stored as a verb that takes to, on the model of decide and want. The learner then produces a sentence saying they paused in order to have a cigarette, which is the opposite of the story.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: to smoke becomes smoking.

errors.wrong: Please remember posting the contract before Friday.
errors.right: Please remember to post the contract before Friday.
errors.why_it_happens: Both patterns exist for remember, so neither trips any alarm. The learner picks the one they use more often and turns an instruction into a claim about the past.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: posting becomes to post.

errors.wrong: We regret telling you that the service will end in June.
errors.right: We regret to tell you that the service will end in June.
errors.why_it_happens: Regret plus -ing is the form the learner meets first and it is the commoner one. Here it turns an apology for the news into an admission that telling you was a mistake.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: telling becomes to tell.

errors.wrong: Widening the road would mean to lose two rows of houses.
errors.right: Widening the road would mean losing two rows of houses.
errors.why_it_happens: Mean is read as intend, and intending takes to. Nobody intends the houses to go; the sentence is about what follows from the plan.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: to lose becomes losing.

pays_in.note: Consequence sentences run on mean plus -ing, and the wrong form reverses the claim.
pays_in.model: Expanding the airport would mean rerouting two rivers and rehousing a village.

pays_in.note: A Part 2 story about a mistake turns on stop, forget and remember.
pays_in.model: I remember checking the locker twice, which is why the whole thing still annoys me.

pays_in.note: A True or False stem often swaps the two patterns and hopes you read straight past it.
pays_in.model: The company went on to open two further sites in the region.

used_in.quote: A story about a mistake is made of forgot, stopped and remembered, and each one has to carry the version that actually happened.
Every solution in this essay has a cost, and cost sentences are built on mean plus an -ing form.

payload.sentence: I stopped taking the bus in about March.
payload.question: Was the speaker a bus user before March?

feedback.why_key: The -ing form points back at a habit that was already running, so it existed to be given up.
feedback.feed_forward: Read -ing after these verbs as something already real.

payload.sentence: The manager remembered to lock the safe before the alarm was set.
payload.question: Was locking the safe something she had to do that night?
options: Yes, it was a task on her list
No, she simply recalled doing it once

feedback.why_key: Remember plus to is about a duty that did not slip, so there was a task before there was a memory.
feedback.feed_forward: Read to plus a verb after these verbs as something that was still ahead.

payload.sentence: Draining the marsh would mean losing the last reed beds in the county.
payload.question: Does anybody want the reed beds to go?

feedback.why_key: Mean plus -ing names what would follow from the plan and says nothing at all about what anyone intends.
feedback.feed_forward: Take mean plus -ing as a consequence, not a wish.

payload.context: A line from a complaints log.
payload.stem: The office forgot ___ (send) the renewal, so the cover lapsed in April.

expected: to send

feedback.why_key: The cover lapsed, so the sending never happened, and only the to-form says that.
feedback.feed_forward: Use forget plus to when the job was never done.

payload.context: Someone giving a friend advice about a slow laptop.
payload.stem: Try ___ (clear) the cache first and see whether that does anything.

expected: clearing

feedback.why_key: See whether that does anything is exactly what try plus -ing means: an experiment, not a struggle.
feedback.feed_forward: Use try plus -ing when you are suggesting a method.

payload.given: The council wants to pedestrianise the high street. Two bus routes would have to be moved.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence saying what the plan would involve.
payload.starter: Pedestrianising the high street would mean ___

expected: moving two bus routes
moving two of the bus routes
moving two bus routes elsewhere

feedback.why_key: The route changes are a consequence of the plan rather than an aim of it, and the -ing form is what says so.
feedback.feed_forward: Put consequences after mean in the -ing form.

payload.audio_text: She'd stopped answering her phone by then.

expected: she'd stopped answering her phone by then
she had stopped answering her phone by then
shed stopped answering her phone by then

feedback.why_key: Stopped answering and stopped to answer differ by one unstressed syllable and describe two different weeks.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for whether a to arrives before the second verb.

items.decision_cue: how her handover got shorter and shorter

payload.context: Priya is describing how her handover got shorter and shorter over the winter.
payload.stem: Halfway through the shift she stopped ___ the notes.

options.why_this_means: That she had been writing notes and gave the writing up.
That she broke off from something else so that she could write them.

expected: writing

feedback.why_key: The story is about a habit shrinking, so the writing was already running and is what came to an end.

items.decision_cue: paused at the desk each time

payload.context: Priya is describing a shift spent moving between beds, where she paused at the desk each time.
payload.stem: Halfway through the shift she stopped ___ the notes.

options.why_this_means: That she had been writing notes and gave the writing up.
That she broke off from something else so that she could write them.

expected: to write

feedback.why_key: The pausing is what stops and the writing is what starts, so the second verb is the thing still ahead.
feedback.feed_forward: Use to when the second verb is what the break was for.

items.decision_cue: confirm that nothing on the list was skipped

payload.context: A supervisor is checking the closing routine and asks him to confirm that nothing on the list was skipped.
payload.stem: He remembered ___ the alarm before he left.

options.why_this_means: That he can picture doing it, which is a claim about his memory.
That the setting was a task he had to do, and it did not slip.

expected: to set

feedback.why_key: The question is whether a duty was carried out, and the to-form is the one that reports a duty met.
feedback.feed_forward: Use remember plus to when a task had to be done.

payload.context: An insurer wants to know what he can actually recall about leaving the building, not what the routine required.
payload.stem: He remembered ___ the alarm before he left.

options.why_this_means: That he can picture doing it, which is a claim about his memory.
That the setting was a task he had to do, and it did not slip.

expected: setting

feedback.why_key: The insurer is asking about a memory of an act, and the -ing form is the one that reports a memory.
feedback.feed_forward: Use remember plus -ing when the act is what is being recalled.

payload.context: Two lines from a note about a missing library book.
sentences: She forgot to return the book.
meanings: The book went back, but she has no memory of taking it.
The book never went back at all.

feedback.why_key: One sentence loses a memory. The other loses a book.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the second verb happened before you choose its form.

payload.context: A support page giving two sensible pieces of advice about a router that keeps dropping.
payload.stem: Try ___ the firmware before you call us.

options.why_this_means: That updating is one method worth an experiment, and it may or may not fix it.
That updating is awkward and the reader is being asked to make the attempt.

follow_up.question: Which version treats the update as an experiment rather than a struggle?

feedback.why_key: Both are real advice. One says this might work; the other says this is hard, please attempt it.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide whether you are offering a method or asking for an effort.

payload.context: From a letter turning down an application.
payload.sentence: We regret telling you that your application has not been successful.
reasons: it says the writer wishes they had not told you
the verb should be in the past
regret cannot take an object at all
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The -ing form makes the telling itself the thing regretted. The letter meant to regret the news.
feedback.feed_forward: Use regret plus to when you are about to deliver bad news.

payload.sentence: Raising the barrage would mean to divert the river for at least two winters.

expected: mean diverting

feedback.why_key: Nobody intends the diversion; it is what the plan would drag in behind it, and that reading needs the -ing form.
feedback.feed_forward: Use mean plus -ing for consequences and mean plus to for intentions.

payload.prompt_text: A city is considering a new ring road. Write one sentence saying what the plan would involve, using mean.

feedback.why_key: A consequence sentence is where this choice pays, and it is the sentence an argument needs straight after a proposal.
feedback.feed_forward: Use mean plus -ing when nobody intends the outcome.

payload.prompt_text: Take the Part 2 card about a mistake you made. Speak for a minute and include one sentence with stopped, forgot or remembered where the form you choose decides what happened. Then say what the other form would have meant.

feedback.why_key: Saying what the other version would have meant is the check that the choice was made rather than guessed.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose the form, then say aloud what the other one would claim.

payload.context: Two versions of the same line in a letter from a training provider.
sentences: We regret telling you that the course is full.
We regret to tell you that the course is full.
meanings: Sending you that message is the thing the writer is sorry about.
The course being full is what the writer is sorry about, and the news is arriving now.

feedback.why_key: One version apologises for the letter. The other apologises for the news, and only one of those was ever meant.
feedback.feed_forward: Use regret to when the sentence is delivering the bad news.

payload.context: Two versions of a line about somebody's career.
sentences: She went on running the Marlow depot for another decade.
She went on to run the Marlow depot for another decade.
meanings: She was already running it, and she stayed at it.
She finished doing something else, and the depot was what came next.

feedback.why_key: One version keeps her where she was. The other moves her into a new job, and one small word does all of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the second verb continues the first or follows it.

payload.context: Two lines from a report on a leisure centre.
sentences: The council meant to close the pool for a fortnight.
Closing the pool meant losing a fortnight's income.
meanings: That was somebody's intention, and an intention can still be dropped.
That was the unavoidable cost of the closure, and nobody chose it.

feedback.why_key: Mean plus to needs a subject that can intend something. Mean plus -ing needs an event that drags a cost behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the subject is capable of intending anything.

points.title: Starting a sentence with an activity instead of a person

teach.can_do: I can make an activity the subject of a sentence, so the sentence is about the doing rather than the doer.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the shortest route out of I think people should and into a sentence that reads as an argument rather than an opinion.
teach.meaning: English lets a verb become the thing a sentence is about by adding -ing. Reducing emissions, teaching children to cook, closing rural branches: each one is an activity handled as a single thing, and each can sit in the subject slot and take a verb of its own. This is not decoration. It lets you talk about what gets done instead of about who does it, which is usually what an argument needs, and it keeps the action visible where a noun would bury it.

form.pattern: -ing form + whatever it takes as its object + a singular verb
notes: the whole -ing phrase counts as one thing, so the verb is singular: closing the branches has cost jobs
to plus a verb can also be a subject, but it sounds formal and slightly old-fashioned in most sentences
no article in front of it: reducing emissions, never the reducing emissions
form.negative: Not being told is the part people mind — the negative goes inside the subject.
form.question: Does reducing emissions actually cost jobs?

right.text: Reducing emissions costs money in the first decade.

spec.caption: The same verb, moved into the subject slot, where it becomes the thing under discussion.

worked_example.sentence: Cutting rural bus services saves less than it costs, once the knock-on effects are counted.
worked_example.why_this_form: The argument is about the cutting itself and not about who does the cutting, and this form puts exactly that in the subject slot.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: When councils cut rural bus services, they save less than it costs drags councils into a sentence that is really about the arithmetic.

notice_set.sentence: Closing the two smallest wards saved under a million pounds.
notice_set.question: What is the sentence reporting on?
notice_set.why: The activity is in the subject slot, so it is the thing the verb is reporting on.

notice_set.sentence: Teaching children to cook takes time that the timetable does not have.
notice_set.question: Who does not have the time?
notice_set.why: The whole activity is the subject, so the sentence can go straight on to what it costs.

notice_set.sentence: Not being told about the change annoyed the whole team.
notice_set.question: Were they told?
notice_set.why: The negative sits inside the subject, and the subject is the thing that annoyed them.

notice_set.sentence: Building on the flood plain has been banned since 2015.
notice_set.question: What has been banned?
notice_set.why: The -ing phrase is what the ban applies to, because it is the subject of the sentence.

notice_set.sentence: Recycling more plastic will not solve the problem on its own.
notice_set.question: Is the sentence saying recycling is useless?
notice_set.why: On its own limits the claim, and the claim is about the activity named in the subject.

teach.rule_line: An -ing phrase in the subject slot is one thing and takes a singular verb.
teach.false_rule: That an -ing subject is informal and an essay should use a noun instead. Both are academic; this one keeps the action visible where a noun hides it.

errors.wrong: Reducing emissions in the transport sector require money that no council has.
errors.right: Reducing emissions in the transport sector requires money that no council has.
errors.why_it_happens: Emissions sits directly in front of the verb and pulls the ending with it. The subject is the whole activity, which is one thing however many emissions are inside it.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: require becomes requires.

errors.wrong: Cutting the number of flights between the two cities by a third.
errors.right: Cutting the number of flights between the two cities by a third would achieve very little.
errors.why_it_happens: The subject phrase is long enough to feel like a whole sentence, and the writer stops when it ends. Nothing has been said about it yet.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one main verb after the subject.

errors.wrong: Reduce emissions is the hardest part of any climate plan.
errors.right: Reducing emissions is the hardest part of any climate plan.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner takes the verb straight from the dictionary and drops it into the subject slot. English will not let a bare verb be a subject; it has to be turned into a thing first.
errors.smallest_fix: Add three letters: reduce becomes reducing.

errors.wrong: Building of new homes on green belt land remains controversial.
errors.right: Building new homes on green belt land remains controversial.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner half-converts the verb into a noun and keeps the of that a real noun would need. The -ing form takes its object directly, with nothing in between.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: of.

pays_in.note: It gives a paragraph an abstract subject without reaching for a nominalisation.
pays_in.model: Charging drivers to enter the centre shifts journeys rather than removing them.

pays_in.note: Trend sentences need the activity itself as the thing being measured.
pays_in.model: Switching away from coal accounts for most of the fall shown after 2012.

pays_in.note: Part 3 answers about society need a subject that is not simply people.
pays_in.model: Working from home has changed what a city centre is actually for.

used_in.quote: Each solution in this essay is an activity, and each one reads better as the subject of its own sentence.
The passage opens several paragraphs with an activity as the subject, which is where the topic of each one sits.

payload.sentence: Insulating older houses cuts more carbon than any new build ever will.
payload.question: What is being compared with new building?

feedback.why_key: The activity holds the subject slot, so the activity is what the comparison is between.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the whole -ing phrase as one thing before you look for the verb.

payload.sentence: Marking two hundred scripts a week leaves very little room for anything else.
payload.question: How many things is the verb agreeing with?

feedback.why_key: The subject is the marking, not the scripts, and one activity takes a singular verb however big it is.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the head of the subject before you check the ending.

items.decision_cue: Replanting the hillsides above the reservoir

payload.context: From a first draft of an essay paragraph.
payload.sentence: Replanting the hillsides above the reservoir over the next fifteen years.
reasons: the subject is there but nothing is said about it
the -ing form should be a bare verb
the sentence needs an article at the front
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The phrase names an activity and then stops. A subject on its own is not a sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Give the -ing subject a verb before the full stop.

payload.context: From a paragraph about household energy.
payload.stem: Replacing old boilers across a whole street ___ (cost) less than most people assume.

expected: costs

feedback.why_key: The subject is the replacing, which is one activity, so the verb takes the singular ending.
feedback.feed_forward: Agree the verb with the activity, not with the nearest noun.

payload.context: From a paragraph about workplace health.
payload.stem: ___ (walk) part of the commute makes more difference than an hour in a gym.

expected: walking

feedback.why_key: A bare verb cannot be a subject, so it has to become a thing first, and -ing is how English does that.
feedback.feed_forward: Turn the verb into an -ing form before you put it in the subject slot.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a city-centre housing scheme.

expected: converting empty offices into flats has housed four hundred families

feedback.why_key: The whole activity comes first as one block, and only then does the sentence get its verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Finish the subject phrase before you start the verb.

payload.given: When councils close rural bus routes, they save very little money.
payload.instruction: Rewrite so that the closing itself is the subject of the sentence.

expected: rural bus routes saves very little money
rural bus routes saves councils very little money
rural bus routes saves very little

feedback.why_key: The councils have left the sentence and the activity has taken their place, which is what the argument was about anyway.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the activity into the subject slot and drop the human subject.

payload.given: People work from home two days a week now. It has changed how the city centre feels.
payload.instruction: Say it in one sentence with the activity as the subject.

expected: has changed how the city centre feels
two days a week has changed how the city centre feels
has changed the way the city centre feels

feedback.why_key: One activity is doing the changing, so the verb stays singular even though it took a crowd of people to do it.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the verb singular after an -ing subject.

payload.audio_text: Raising wages hasn't closed the gap on its own.

expected: raising wages hasn't closed the gap on its own
raising wages has not closed the gap on its own
raising wages hasnt closed the gap on its own

feedback.why_key: Hasn't and haven't sound close at speed, and the one you write says whether you heard the subject as one thing or many.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the singular auxiliary after an -ing subject.

items.decision_cue: in the two largest cities have

payload.sentence: Banning older diesel vehicles in the two largest cities have made almost no difference to roadside readings.

expected: cities has made

feedback.why_key: The subject is the banning, not the cities. Two cities sit next to the verb and steal the agreement.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace the verb back to the -ing form before choosing its ending.

payload.prompt_text: Write one sentence about a way of cutting household waste, making the activity itself the subject and saying what it achieves.

feedback.why_key: Putting the activity first makes the sentence a claim about the activity, which is what a body paragraph argues over.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with the activity, then say what it does.

payload.prompt_text: Rewrite the solutions paragraph of your sedentary-working-day answer so that two sentences open with an activity as the subject. Check the verb after each one. Four minutes.

feedback.why_key: A solutions paragraph built on activities argues about what works. One built on people argues about who to blame.
feedback.feed_forward: Open two sentences with an activity, then check both verbs.

points.title: Getting the small word right after an adjective

teach.can_do: I can put the right preposition after an adjective and the right verb form after that preposition.
teach.why_it_matters: Two mistakes stacked inside three words, and both are visible. They cost lexical marks as well as grammar marks, which is why fixing them pays twice.
teach.meaning: Many adjectives will not stand next to a verb on their own. They need a preposition first, and which preposition is decided by the adjective rather than by the meaning: responsible for, capable of, committed to, involved in, aware of, keen on, dependent on. Once the preposition is in place, whatever follows it has to be a noun or an -ing form, because that is all a preposition will take. The two rules meet inside the same three words, which is why the errors come in pairs.

notes: the preposition belongs to the adjective and has to be learned with it, like a second syllable
committed to and dedicated to end in to, and that to is a preposition, so -ing follows it
aware of, capable of, guilty of; responsible for, famous for, known for; involved in, interested in, successful in
form.negative: Not responsible for cutting — the not goes in front of the adjective, never in front of the preposition.
form.question: Who is responsible for approving the budget?

left.role: the adjective and its own preposition

spec.caption: Two fixed choices in a row: which preposition, and then which verb form.

worked_example.sentence: The trust is responsible for cutting the waiting list by a third this year.
worked_example.why_this_form: Responsible carries for wherever it goes, and once for is in place the verb has no choice left: it becomes cutting.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Responsible to cut is not a different meaning. It is a sentence that stops making sense at the preposition and has to be reread.

notice_set.sentence: She is capable of running the whole depot on her own.
notice_set.question: Is she running it now?
notice_set.why: Capable of names an ability, not a current arrangement.

notice_set.sentence: The firm is committed to reducing packaging by 2030.
notice_set.question: What has the firm promised?
notice_set.why: Committed to takes what follows as a thing promised, which is why the verb turns into an -ing form.

notice_set.sentence: Nobody was aware of the change until Friday.
notice_set.question: Did people know before Friday?
notice_set.why: Aware of takes a thing, and the thing here is the change.

notice_set.sentence: Two departments are involved in checking the figures.
notice_set.question: How many departments do the checking?
notice_set.why: Involved in takes the activity, and the -ing form is what the preposition allows.

notice_set.sentence: The town is famous for making rope.
notice_set.question: Is the town doing something, or known for something?
notice_set.why: Famous for names what the place is known for, and for takes an -ing form.

teach.rule_line: Learn the preposition with the adjective, then let it force the -ing.
teach.false_rule: That the preposition can be worked out from the meaning. It cannot. Good at and skilled in mean nearly the same thing and take different words.

errors.wrong: The department is responsible of approving new contracts.
errors.right: The department is responsible for approving new contracts.
errors.why_it_happens: Of is the commonest preposition after an adjective, so it arrives by default whenever the stored pair is missing. Nothing about the meaning would warn the learner off it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: of becomes for.

errors.wrong: The company is committed to reduce its packaging by a third.
errors.right: The company is committed to reducing its packaging by a third.
errors.why_it_happens: The to looks like the to of an infinitive, and every instinct the learner has says a bare verb follows it. Here it is a preposition, and prepositions do not take bare verbs.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: reduce becomes reducing.

errors.wrong: She is very good in explaining things to new staff.
errors.right: She is very good at explaining things to new staff.
errors.why_it_happens: In is right after successful and skilled, and the learner generalises across a group of adjectives that look interchangeable and are not.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: in becomes at.

errors.wrong: They are responsible for the reduce of waste on site.
errors.right: They are responsible for reducing waste on site.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows a noun can follow a preposition and goes looking for one, but reduce is not a noun. The -ing form is the noun this verb already has.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one phrase: the reduce of becomes reducing.

pays_in.note: Responsibility and capability sentences are the spine of a solutions paragraph.
pays_in.model: Employers are capable of cutting commuting without cutting anybody's hours.

pays_in.note: Part 3 keeps asking who should be responsible for what.
pays_in.model: Schools are better at teaching this than most parents are, honestly.

pays_in.note: A letter of complaint has to name who is responsible for what.
pays_in.model: I understand the agency is responsible for arranging repairs of this kind.

used_in.quote: The essay has to say who is capable of what and who is responsible for what, which is this pattern half a dozen times.
Questions about who should give advice are answered with adjectives that all carry their own preposition.

payload.sentence: The site manager is responsible for checking every load before it leaves.
payload.question: Who does the checking?

feedback.why_key: Responsible for names the duty, and the person carrying it is the subject of the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the adjective and its preposition as one unit.

payload.sentence: The operator is committed to cutting its water use by a fifth.
payload.question: Has the cut already happened?

feedback.why_key: Committed to names a promise, so the cutting is still in front of them rather than behind them.
feedback.feed_forward: Treat the to in committed to as a preposition, not an infinitive.

payload.context: From a first draft of a paragraph about staff retention.
payload.sentence: The firm says it is committed to increase pay for its lowest-paid staff.
reasons: the to here is a preposition, so an -ing form has to follow it
the adjective needs a different preposition
the verb should be in the past
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Committed carries to as its own preposition, and prepositions never take a bare verb.
feedback.feed_forward: After committed to, write the -ing form.

payload.context: From a note on who signs off what.
payload.stem: The finance team is responsible ___ approving anything over five thousand pounds.

expected: for

feedback.why_key: Responsible carries for and nothing else, which is why the pair has to be stored as one item.
feedback.feed_forward: Store responsible for as a single chunk.

payload.context: From a paragraph about coastal defences.
payload.stem: Older sea walls are simply not capable of ___ (hold) back a surge of that size.

expected: holding

feedback.why_key: Of is a preposition, and a preposition takes the -ing form whatever the verb happens to be.
feedback.feed_forward: Put -ing on the verb straight after the preposition.

payload.context: Someone talking about a course they are on.
payload.stem: I've always been quite good ___ picking up the grammar, it's the speaking that goes.

expected: at

feedback.why_key: Good takes at, and no amount of thinking about ability will produce it. It has to be remembered.
feedback.feed_forward: Learn good at as one chunk, like a two-word adjective.

payload.given: The trust will reduce waiting times by a third. It has said so publicly.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence using committed and the right two words after it.

expected: to reducing waiting times by a third
to cutting waiting times by a third

feedback.why_key: The to belongs to committed rather than to the verb, so the verb has to arrive as an -ing form.
feedback.feed_forward: Write committed to, then add -ing to the verb.

payload.audio_text: We're not really involved in running the site any more.

expected: we're not really involved in running the site any more
we are not really involved in running the site any more
were not really involved in running the site any more

feedback.why_key: The preposition is unstressed and sits between two longer words, which is exactly where a small word goes missing.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the little word between the adjective and the -ing.

payload.sentence: The whole restoration project is dependent of continued funding from the regional authority.

expected: dependent on
dependent upon

feedback.why_key: Depend on is known, but the adjective is stored separately and picks up of from the crowd around it.
feedback.feed_forward: Carry the preposition across from the verb you already know.

payload.context: From a draft paragraph about how firms recruit.
payload.sentence: Line managers are now responsible of hiring their own teams.
reasons: the adjective takes a different preposition
the verb after the preposition is the wrong form
the subject and verb do not agree
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The -ing form after the preposition is right. It is the preposition itself that the adjective refuses.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the preposition first, then the verb form.

payload.sentence: Far more adults are interested in learn a second language than actually enrol.

expected: interested in learning

feedback.why_key: The preposition is right and the verb form is not, which is the other half of the same three-word problem.
feedback.feed_forward: Add -ing to any verb that follows a preposition.

payload.prompt_text: Write one sentence about who should deal with long working hours, using responsible for or capable of and an -ing form after it.

feedback.why_key: Naming who is responsible and for what is how a solutions paragraph stops being a wish list.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the adjective, its preposition, then the -ing form.

payload.prompt_text: Write the solutions paragraph of the sedentary-working-day essay using three different adjective-plus-preposition pairs. Underline each preposition and check the form after it. Four minutes.

feedback.why_key: Three pairs in one paragraph is where the habit either holds or comes apart, and it comes apart in the same two places every time.
feedback.feed_forward: Check every preposition, then every verb form after it.

points.title: Saying who made, let or helped somebody do something

point_json.grammar_name: make, let, have, get and help + object + verb form

teach.can_do: I can use make, let, have, get and help correctly, even though each one takes a different form after its object.
teach.why_it_matters: Five extremely common verbs, five different shapes, and no rule joining them. Getting one wrong is audible in the first minute of a speaking test.
teach.meaning: This is a closed set, and it has to be memorised rather than worked out. All five say that one person brings about an action by somebody else, and they differ in how much pressure is applied and in what form the second verb takes. Make and let take a bare verb. Have takes a bare verb when you are arranging something as a matter of course. Get takes to, because it means persuading. Help takes either, and nobody minds which one you pick.

form.pattern: make / let / have + object + bare verb; get + object + to + verb; help + object + (to) + verb
notes: make somebody do, let somebody do, have somebody do — no to anywhere
get somebody to do is the only member of the group that keeps the to
help somebody do and help somebody to do are both correct English
in the passive, make picks the to back up: staff were made to sign
form.negative: Let does not go negative comfortably; use not allow instead: the rules do not allow staff to leave early.
form.question: What made you change your mind?

spec.label: how much pressure is being applied?

steps.gloss: you arrange it as a matter of course

worked_example.sentence: The head let the sixth form run the open evening themselves.
worked_example.why_this_form: Let takes the bare verb, with nothing standing between the students and the running, and that bareness is part of what the verb means: no pressure applied.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Let the sixth form to run is not a softer version of the same sentence. It is a sentence the reader stumbles over and has to repair before carrying on.

notice_set.sentence: The school made every pupil sit the test again.
notice_set.question: Did the pupils have a choice?
notice_set.why: Make is the strongest of the five, and the bare verb goes straight after the object.

notice_set.sentence: She got two colleagues to check the figures.
notice_set.question: Did she check them herself?
notice_set.why: Get names persuading somebody else, and it is the one verb here that keeps its to.

notice_set.sentence: They had the surveyor come back on Friday.
notice_set.question: Who came back?
notice_set.why: The object is the person who acts, and the verb after it arrives bare.

notice_set.sentence: He helped his sister move the boxes.
notice_set.question: How many people moved boxes?
notice_set.why: Help means both were involved, and the verb after the object can go bare.

notice_set.sentence: Staff were made to sign a new contract.
notice_set.question: Did they want to?
notice_set.why: The passive of make brings the to back, and the sentence reports pressure without reporting anyone's feelings.

teach.rule_line: Make, let and have take a bare verb; get takes to; help takes either.
teach.false_rule: That these five behave alike because they mean nearly the same thing. Meaning does not decide the pattern here. The individual verb does, and there are only five to learn.

errors.wrong: The new rules make staff to log every visitor.
errors.right: The new rules make staff log every visitor.
errors.why_it_happens: Make is being treated like force and require, which do take to. The learner has generalised from a much larger group onto one of the few exceptions.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: to.

errors.wrong: Her supervisor let her to leave an hour early.
errors.right: Her supervisor let her leave an hour early.
errors.why_it_happens: Let sits in the mind right next to allow, and allow takes an object and to. The two verbs are near-synonyms with different shapes, and nothing in the meaning warns you.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: to.

errors.wrong: We finally got the landlord fix the boiler.
errors.right: We finally got the landlord to fix the boiler.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has stored make and let correctly and extends the bare verb across the whole group. Get is the one member that wants its to kept.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: to.

errors.wrong: The scheme helps students to finding work in the region.
errors.right: The scheme helps students find work in the region.
errors.why_it_happens: Two patterns are being merged: help plus to plus a verb, and a preposition plus an -ing form. Only one of them can be right at a time.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one phrase: to finding becomes find.

pays_in.note: Part 1 answers about school and family run on made me and let me.
pays_in.model: My parents let me choose the subjects, which not everyone gets.

pays_in.note: Policy sentences need the difference between making people act and helping them.
pays_in.model: Fining drivers makes them slow down; better lighting helps them see the junction.

pays_in.note: A speaker's attitude often sits in which of the five they reach for.
pays_in.model: They had the whole team come in on the Saturday.

used_in.quote: Answers about what a course or a job requires of you come out as made me, let me and got me to.
The essay has to distinguish between forcing drivers out of the centre and helping them leave the car behind.

payload.sentence: My parents let me drop chemistry after the first year.
payload.question: Did the speaker want to drop it?

feedback.why_key: Let means permission was given for something the speaker was after, which is why no pressure is anywhere in the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Read let as permission and make as pressure.

payload.sentence: The auditor got two of the managers to reopen the files.
payload.question: Who reopened the files?

feedback.why_key: Get names persuading, so the work was done by the people named after the verb rather than by the person applying the pressure.
feedback.feed_forward: The object of these verbs is always the one who acts.

payload.context: From a first draft of a paragraph about shift patterns.
payload.sentence: Some contracts still make employees to work six days in a row.
reasons: make does not take to before the second verb
the object should come after the second verb
the main verb should be in the past
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Make takes the bare verb. The to has arrived from force and require, which are not in this group.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete to after make and let.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a change to the timetable.
payload.stem: The new rule makes every pupil ___ (choose) a practical subject in the third year.

expected: choose

feedback.why_key: Make takes the verb bare, with nothing at all between the pupil and the choosing.
feedback.feed_forward: After make, write the verb with no to in front of it.

payload.context: Someone talking about growing up in a big household.
payload.stem: It took us weeks to get my father ___ (agree) to a shared calendar.

expected: to agree

feedback.why_key: Get is the one verb in the group that keeps its to, and weeks of persuading is exactly what it means.
feedback.feed_forward: After get, keep the to.

payload.context: From a letter about work on a flat.
payload.stem: I would like to have an engineer ___ (inspect) the boiler before the winter.

expected: inspect

feedback.why_key: Have used for arranging something takes the bare verb, the same as make and let.
feedback.feed_forward: After have, leave the verb bare.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a depot training week.

expected: the training helped the new drivers read the route cards faster

feedback.why_key: Help takes the object first and then the verb, and the verb can go bare with nothing lost.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the person straight after help, then the verb.

payload.audio_text: They wouldn't let us take the books home.

expected: they wouldn't let us take the books home
they would not let us take the books home
they wouldnt let us take the books home

feedback.why_key: Let us take runs together at speed, and if you hear a to that is not there you will write one.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the gap where a to would be, and leave it empty after let.

payload.sentence: The agency would not let us to move in until the certificate had come through.

expected: let us move

feedback.why_key: Let refuses the to, however much it looks like allow. The two verbs mean the same and are built differently.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete to after let.

items.decision_cue: got the whole department fill in

payload.sentence: In the end she got the whole department fill in the same form twice.

expected: department to fill in

feedback.why_key: Getting a department to do anything is persuasion, and persuasion is the one meaning in this group that keeps its to.
feedback.feed_forward: Insert to after the object when the verb is get.

payload.context: From a draft paragraph about a work-placement scheme.
payload.sentence: The scheme helps students to finding paid work in their final year.
reasons: two patterns have been mixed and the verb form is wrong
help cannot take an object at all
the subject and the verb do not agree
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Help takes find or to find. What it will not take is a to with an -ing form behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: After help, choose the bare verb or to plus the verb, never both patterns at once.

payload.prompt_text: Say one thing your family made you do as a child and one thing they let you do. Two clauses, one sentence.

feedback.why_key: Made and let side by side is where the shared bare verb becomes obvious, and where a stray to would stand out.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the bare verb after both made and let.

payload.prompt_text: Answer the Part 1 questions about your work or studies. Somewhere in your answers, use make, let and get about the people around you, and keep the form right on each one. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: These three arrive early in a speaking test and they arrive fast, which is the only condition under which the pattern really has to be automatic.
feedback.feed_forward: Bare verb after make and let, to after get.
